Lucía applies for a summer job as a tour guide. Mr Ruiz, from the agency “Madrid Secreto”, interviews her.
Good morning, Lucía. Please take a seat. Tell me a little about yourself.
Good morning. I’m twenty and I’m studying Tourism at the Complutense University. I’m in my third year.
Do you have any experience as a guide?
Yes. Last summer I worked for two months as a guide at the Prado Museum.
And for the past year I’ve been giving Spanish lessons to foreigners at weekends.
Very interesting. What languages do you speak?
Spanish, English and French. And I’m learning Italian.
I’m responsible, very organised and I’m very good at public speaking. I love working with people.
Sometimes I’m too much of a perfectionist. And I’m hopeless with maps… but I never get lost in Madrid!
Ha, ha. The job is part-time, from July to September, in the mornings. The salary is nine hundred euros a month.
On the first of July. We’ll call you this week with an answer. It’s been a pleasure, Lucía.
“desde hace un año” = for a year
“se me da bien” = I’m good at
“se me dan fatal” = I’m hopeless at
Currículum: rolled rr, stressed on “RRÍ”. Many people just say “el CV” = “el the-OO-beh”.
Polite imperatives with pronouns: HÁ-ble-me, SIÉN-te-se. Stress on the first syllable.
Experiencia = “es-pe-ryen-thya” (x before a consonant is read s), extranjeros = “es-tran-he-ros”.
1. Experience in a CV: which tense do you use?
experience with no date / in general
Trabajo aquí desde hace dos años.
The interview question “¿Ha trabajado alguna vez en…?” takes the perfecto in the answer if you give no date: “Sí, he trabajado…”. If you give the date: “Sí, trabajé allí en 2022”.
Three time expressions that confuse everyone:
I’ve worked here for two years.
With “desde hace” you use the PRESENT (the thing is still going on), where English uses the present perfect (“I’ve worked”). With “hace” alone you use the INDEFINIDO (a finished action).
3. “Se me da bien”: what you’re good at
A very Spanish expression, built like GUSTAR: the thing “is given well” or “badly” to you.
Alternatives: Soy bueno/a en… (I’m good at), Tengo experiencia en… (I have experience in), Sé + infinitive (I know how to): Sé programar.
Soy responsable, organizado/a… Se me da bien…
A veces soy demasiado… Estoy mejorando…
¿Dónde se ve dentro de cinco años?
Dentro de cinco años me gustaría…
5. What you ask at the end
“Empezaría”, “me gustaría”, “podría”: this form (the conditional) is very polite. You learn it fully in chapter 27.
In an interview use USTED, unless the other person suggests tú (“Puedes tutearme” = You can call me tú).
He trabajado en un hotel en 2023.

On the first of July Lucía woke up at half past six, two hours earlier than usual. It was her first day as a guide at the “Madrid Secreto” agency.
She had prepared a lot: she had studied the history of every street and practised her presentation in front of the mirror.
At nine she arrived at Puerta del Sol. Mr Ruiz was waiting there with her first group: twenty tourists from six different countries.
“Today you’re on your own,” he told her. “I trust you.” Lucía swallowed hard. Her hands were shaking a little.
She began the tour in English. She explained that Puerta del Sol is Spain’s kilometre zero and that people eat the New Year’s Eve grapes there.
Then a French couple asked her a question in French. Lucía answered in French with no problem. She was good at languages!
Everything was going perfectly until they reached Plaza Mayor. There, an eight-year-old Japanese boy disappeared.
His mother started shouting. Lucía panicked, but she remembered something her grandmother had taught her: “In difficult moments, breathe and think.”
She breathed. She thought. What interests an eight-year-old in Plaza Mayor?
She looked around and saw a shop selling comics and superhero figures. She ran over, and there was the boy, staring at the window with his mouth open.
The mother hugged her and thanked her many times in Japanese. Lucía understood just one word: “arigatō”. Thanks to Kenji, she knew what it meant.
The rest of the tour was calm. They finished at the Royal Palace at half past one.
At the end, the tourists applauded and left very good reviews on the agency’s page.
One of them said: “Lucía is the best guide in Madrid. She knows history, speaks four languages… and finds lost children!”.
In the afternoon Mr Ruiz called her. “I’ve read the reviews,” he said. “Would you like to work with us in September too?”
Lucía didn’t hesitate for a second.
¿Qué le ofreció el señor Ruiz al final?
I worked in a bank for five years.
